questions.prompt: Define electric current.
questions.answer: The rate of flow of electric charge.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating current, charge and time.
questions.answer: I = ΔQ/Δt (current = charge flow ÷ time taken).

questions.prompt: State the unit of electric charge and its symbol.
questions.answer: The coulomb (C).

questions.prompt: State the direction of conventional current relative to the flow of electrons in a metal wire.
questions.answer: Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to the direction of electron flow.

questions.prompt: Describe how charge is carried through a metal wire and through an electrolyte.
questions.answer: In a metal, charge is carried by free electrons; in an electrolyte, it is carried by positive and negative ions.

title: Charge quantisation and Kirchhoff's first law

questions.prompt: State the value of the elementary charge e.
State the charge of an electron and the charge of a proton in terms of e.
questions.answer: Electron: −e; proton: +e.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by saying that electric charge is quantised.
questions.answer: Charge exists only in discrete amounts that are whole-number multiples of the elementary charge e, so the net charge on a particle or object is a multiple of e.

questions.prompt: State Kirchhoff's first law.
questions.answer: The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving that junction.

questions.prompt: State the physical principle that Kirchhoff's first law is a consequence of.
questions.answer: The conservation of charge.

questions.prompt: A particle has a net charge of +3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate its charge in terms of e.
Define the mean drift velocity of charge carriers in a conductor.
questions.answer: The average velocity of the charge carriers along the conductor in the direction of current flow.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating current to mean drift velocity.
questions.answer: I = Anev, where A is the cross-sectional area, n is the number density, e is the elementary charge and v is the mean drift velocity.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the number density n of charge carriers.
questions.answer: The number of charge carriers per unit volume of the material.

questions.prompt: State the unit of number density.
questions.answer: m⁻³ (per cubic metre).

questions.prompt: State how the number density of charge carriers in a conductor compares with that in a semiconductor and in an insulator.
questions.answer: It is very large in a conductor, much smaller in a semiconductor and extremely small in an insulator.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the mean drift velocity of the electrons in a wire when the current is increased, for the same wire.
questions.answer: It increases; the mean drift velocity is directly proportional to the current.

questions.prompt: Name the component represented in a circuit diagram by a rectangle.
questions.answer: A resistor.

questions.prompt: Name the component represented in a circuit diagram by a circle containing a cross.
questions.answer: A lamp.

questions.prompt: Name the component represented in a circuit diagram by two parallel lines of equal length.
questions.answer: A capacitor.

questions.prompt: Name the component represented in a circuit diagram by a triangle with a line across its tip.
questions.answer: A diode.

questions.prompt: Name the component represented by a diode symbol with two arrows pointing away from it.
questions.answer: A light-emitting diode (LED).

questions.prompt: State why standard circuit symbols are used in circuit diagrams.
questions.answer: So that circuits are represented clearly and unambiguously, and can be understood by anyone regardless of language.

questions.prompt: Define potential difference.
questions.answer: The energy transferred per unit charge when electrical energy is converted into other forms of energy.

questions.prompt: Define the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source.
questions.answer: The energy transferred per unit charge when other forms of energy are converted into electrical energy.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a potential difference of one volt.
questions.answer: One joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating energy transferred, charge and potential difference.
questions.answer: W = VQ.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating energy transferred, charge and e.m.f.
questions.answer: W = EQ.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between e.m.f. and potential difference in terms of energy transfer.
questions.answer: E.m.f. is the energy transferred from other forms into electrical energy per unit charge in the source; p.d. is the energy transferred from electrical energy into other forms per unit charge across a component.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference V to its speed.
questions.answer: eV = ½mv².

questions.prompt: Define resistance.
questions.answer: The opposition to the flow of electric current, defined as the potential difference across a component divided by the current through it.

questions.prompt: State the equation for resistance in terms of potential difference and current.
questions.answer: R = V/I.

questions.prompt: State the unit of resistance.
questions.answer: The ohm (Ω), equal to one volt per ampere (V/A).

questions.prompt: State Ohm's law.
questions.answer: The current through an ohmic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided its temperature remains constant.

questions.prompt: State the condition that must be satisfied for Ohm's law to apply to a conductor.
questions.answer: The temperature of the conductor must remain constant.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a non-ohmic component.
questions.answer: A component whose resistance changes with the current through it, so its I–V graph is not a straight line through the origin.

questions.prompt: State what the gradient of an I–V graph represents when current is plotted on the y-axis and potential difference on the x-axis.
questions.answer: The conductance, 1/R (the reciprocal of the resistance).

questions.prompt: State the shape of the I–V characteristic of a resistor at constant temperature.
questions.answer: A straight line through the origin.

questions.prompt: State how the resistance of a filament lamp changes as the potential difference across it increases.
questions.answer: It increases.

questions.prompt: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current through it increases.
questions.answer: The filament's temperature rises, so its ions vibrate more and collide with the charge carriers more frequently, increasing the resistance.

questions.prompt: State how a diode behaves when it is reverse biased.
questions.answer: It has a very high resistance and allows (almost) no current to flow.

questions.prompt: State the approximate potential difference needed for a silicon diode to start conducting in the forward direction.
questions.answer: About 0.6 V.

questions.prompt: Name the component that has an I–V characteristic similar to a diode but emits light when it conducts.
questions.answer: A light-emitting diode (LED).

questions.prompt: State how the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) changes as light intensity increases.
questions.answer: It decreases.

questions.prompt: State how the resistance of a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor changes as its temperature increases.
questions.answer: It decreases.

questions.prompt: State one way to reduce the heating effect when measuring the I–V characteristic of a filament lamp.
questions.answer: Keep the current small (increase the potential difference in small steps and switch off between readings).

questions.prompt: State the equation relating resistance to resistivity, length and cross-sectional area.
questions.answer: R = ρL/A.

questions.prompt: State the unit of resistivity.
questions.answer: The ohm metre (Ω m).

questions.prompt: Define resistivity.
questions.answer: The resistance of a piece of the material of unit length and unit cross-sectional area (ρ = RA/L).

questions.prompt: State how the resistivity of a metal changes as its temperature increases.
questions.answer: It increases.

questions.prompt: State how the resistivity of a semiconductor changes as its temperature increases.
questions.answer: It decreases.

questions.prompt: Explain why the resistivity of a semiconductor decreases as its temperature increases.
questions.answer: More charge carriers are released as thermal energy breaks bonds, so the number density of charge carriers increases and the resistivity falls.

questions.prompt: State one way to reduce random error when measuring the diameter of a wire in a resistivity experiment.
questions.answer: Measure the diameter at several points along the wire and take an average.

questions.prompt: State three equations for electrical power.
questions.answer: P = VI, P = I²R and P = V²/R.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the energy transferred by an electrical component in terms of potential difference, current and time.
questions.answer: W = VIt.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a kilowatt-hour.
questions.answer: The energy transferred by a device of power 1 kW operating for 1 hour.

questions.prompt: State the number of joules in one kilowatt-hour.
Calculate the energy transferred by a 2 kW heater used for 3 hours. Give your answer in kWh.
State how the cost of electrical energy is calculated from the energy used and the cost per kilowatt-hour.
questions.answer: Cost = energy used in kWh × cost per kWh.

questions.prompt: Calculate the power of a device that transfers 600 J of energy in 30 s.
State Kirchhoff's second law.
questions.answer: The sum of the e.m.f.s around any closed loop equals the sum of the potential differences around that loop.

questions.prompt: State the physical principle that Kirchhoff's second law is a consequence of.
questions.answer: The conservation of energy.

questions.prompt: State the total e.m.f. of two identical 1.5 V cells connected in series in the same direction.
State the net e.m.f. of a 2.0 V cell and a 1.5 V cell connected in series in opposition.
State the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in series.
questions.answer: R = R₁ + R₂ (the total is the sum of the individual resistances).

questions.prompt: State the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in parallel.
State how the current through components connected in series compares.
questions.answer: The current is the same through each component.

questions.prompt: State how the potential differences across parallel branches compare.
questions.answer: They are equal; the same potential difference is across each branch.

questions.prompt: State how the total resistance of a circuit changes when another resistor is added in parallel.
questions.answer: It decreases.

questions.prompt: Explain why adding a resistor in parallel decreases the total resistance of a circuit.
questions.answer: The extra branch provides another path for current, so the total current from the supply increases for the same potential difference, meaning the total resistance is lower.

questions.prompt: State how the total resistance of two resistors in parallel compares with the smaller of the two resistances.
questions.answer: It is always less than the smaller resistance.

questions.prompt: State how the potential difference across the larger of two resistors in series compares with that across the smaller resistor.
questions.answer: It is larger; the larger resistance takes a larger share of the supply potential difference.

questions.prompt: Define the internal resistance of a source of e.m.f.
questions.answer: The resistance of the components inside the source that oppose the flow of current through it.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the terminal potential difference of a source.
questions.answer: The potential difference across the terminals of the source when it is supplying current.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by 'lost volts'.
questions.answer: The potential difference across the internal resistance (the energy dissipated per unit charge inside the source), equal to Ir.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating e.m.f., terminal potential difference, current and internal resistance.
questions.answer: E = V + Ir.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the e.m.f. of a source in terms of the total resistance of the circuit.
questions.answer: E = I(R + r).

questions.prompt: State what happens to the terminal potential difference of a cell as the current drawn from it increases.
questions.answer: It decreases, because the lost volts increase.

questions.prompt: State what the intercept and the gradient of a graph of terminal potential difference against current represent.
questions.answer: The intercept is the e.m.f. E and the gradient is −r (the negative of the internal resistance).

questions.prompt: State the potential divider equation for the output potential difference across resistor R₂ when it is in series with R₁.
questions.answer: Vout = R₂/(R₁ + R₂) × Vin.

questions.prompt: State the ratio equation for the potential differences across two resistors in series.
questions.answer: V₁/V₂ = R₁/R₂.

questions.prompt: State the purpose of a potential divider circuit.
questions.answer: To split a supply potential difference into smaller, controllable potential differences.

questions.prompt: State what a potentiometer is.
questions.answer: A variable potential divider — a resistor with a sliding contact that taps off a variable fraction of the supply potential difference.

questions.prompt: State how the output potential difference across R₂ changes when the resistance of R₂ is increased, with R₁ and the supply potential difference fixed.
questions.answer: It increases.

questions.prompt: Explain how a thermistor in a potential divider can produce a potential difference that changes with temperature.
questions.answer: As the temperature rises, the thermistor's resistance falls, so the share of the supply potential difference across it changes and the output potential difference across the other resistor changes.

questions.prompt: An LDR forms the upper resistor of a potential divider. State how the potential difference across the lower fixed resistor changes as light intensity increases.
questions.answer: It increases, because the LDR's resistance falls and it takes a smaller share of the supply potential difference.

questions.prompt: Define the displacement of a point on a wave.
questions.answer: The distance of the point from its equilibrium position, in a stated direction.

questions.prompt: Define the amplitude of a wave.
questions.answer: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position.

questions.prompt: Define the wavelength of a wave.
questions.answer: The distance between two adjacent corresponding points on the wave that are in phase (for example, two successive crests).

questions.prompt: Define the frequency of a wave.
questions.answer: The number of complete oscillations passing a point per second.

questions.prompt: Define the period of a wave.
questions.answer: The time taken for one complete oscillation (one cycle).

questions.prompt: Define the phase difference between two points on a wave.
questions.answer: The difference in the stage of the cycle reached by the two points, measured as an angle in radians or degrees.

questions.prompt: State the phase difference between two points on a wave separated by one wavelength.
questions.answer: 360° (2π radians); the two points are in phase.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the speed of a wave.
questions.answer: The distance travelled by the wave per unit time (the speed at which energy is transferred by the wave).

questions.prompt: State how the frequency of a wave can be determined from a cathode-ray oscilloscope trace.
questions.answer: Measure the time for one complete cycle using the time-base setting, then calculate f = 1/T.

title: Progressive waves and the wave equation

questions.prompt: Define a progressive wave.
questions.answer: A wave that transfers energy from one place to another as it travels, without transferring matter.

questions.prompt: State the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
questions.answer: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating frequency and period.
State the wave equation.
questions.answer: v = fλ.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the speed of a wave if its frequency is doubled while its wavelength remains constant.
questions.answer: The speed doubles (v ∝ f at constant λ).

questions.prompt: Describe the shape of a displacement–distance graph for a transverse wave.
questions.answer: A sine (or cosine) curve, oscillating about the equilibrium position with constant amplitude and wavelength.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by reflection of a wave.
questions.answer: The wave bounces off a boundary, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by refraction of a wave.
questions.answer: The change in speed and direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by diffraction of a wave.
questions.answer: The spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle.

questions.prompt: State the condition for diffraction to be significant.
questions.answer: The wavelength must be comparable to the size of the gap or obstacle.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by polarisation of a wave.
questions.answer: The restriction of the wave's oscillations to one plane.

questions.prompt: State which type of wave can be polarised.
questions.answer: Transverse waves only.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the intensity of a wave.
questions.answer: I = P/A (power per unit area).

questions.prompt: State how the intensity of a wave changes if its amplitude is doubled.
questions.answer: It becomes four times greater (I ∝ amplitude²).

questions.prompt: State what a ripple tank can be used to demonstrate.
questions.answer: Wave properties such as reflection, refraction and diffraction, using water waves.

questions.prompt: State the order of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength.
questions.answer: Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves.

questions.prompt: State the order of magnitude of the wavelength of visible light.
questions.answer: About 10⁻⁷ m (400–700 nm).

questions.prompt: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
questions.answer: They are transverse, and they travel at the speed of light in a vacuum (they can travel through a vacuum).

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a plane polarised electromagnetic wave.
questions.answer: A wave whose electric field oscillations are restricted to one plane.

questions.prompt: State how the polarisation of microwaves can be demonstrated using a metal grille.
questions.answer: Rotating the grille between the transmitter and receiver changes the received intensity; the wave is transmitted when the grille's slits are parallel to its electric field oscillations.

questions.prompt: State why the polarisation of light shows that light is a transverse wave.
questions.answer: Only transverse waves can be polarised; longitudinal waves cannot.

questions.prompt: State how a polarising filter affects unpolarised light.
questions.answer: It transmits only the component of the oscillations in one plane, so the transmitted light is plane polarised and its intensity is reduced.

title: Refraction, refractive index and total internal reflection

questions.prompt: Define the refractive index of a medium.
questions.answer: The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the medium, n = c/v.

questions.prompt: State Snell's law.
questions.answer: n₁ sin i₁ = n₂ sin i₂, where the angles are measured to the normal.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the critical angle.
questions.answer: The angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is exactly 90°.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the critical angle at a boundary between a medium of refractive index n and air.
questions.answer: sin C = 1/n.

questions.prompt: State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection.
questions.answer: Light must travel from a more optically dense medium to a less optically dense medium, and the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle.

questions.prompt: State how the speed of light in a medium changes as the refractive index of the medium increases.
questions.answer: It decreases (v = c/n).

questions.prompt: State what happens to the frequency and to the wavelength of light when it passes into a medium of higher refractive index.
questions.answer: The frequency stays the same and the wavelength decreases.

questions.prompt: State the apparatus used to investigate refraction of light through a glass block.
questions.answer: A ray box, a glass block and a protractor (to measure the angles).

questions.prompt: State the principle of superposition.
questions.answer: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.

questions.prompt: Define coherence.
questions.answer: Two waves have a constant phase difference and the same frequency.

questions.prompt: Define interference.
questions.answer: The superposition of two or more waves to produce a resultant wave whose amplitude depends on the phase difference between them.

questions.prompt: State the condition for constructive interference in terms of path difference.
questions.answer: The path difference is a whole-number multiple of the wavelength, nλ (for example 0, λ or 2λ).

questions.prompt: State the condition for destructive interference in terms of path difference.
questions.answer: The path difference is an odd-number multiple of half a wavelength, (n + ½)λ.

questions.prompt: State the phase difference that corresponds to a path difference of half a wavelength.
questions.answer: 180° (π radians).

questions.prompt: State what is meant by path difference.
questions.answer: The difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to a given point.

questions.prompt: Give one example of a two-source interference experiment using sound or microwaves.
questions.answer: Two loudspeakers driven by the same signal produce alternating loud and quiet regions (or two microwave sources produce maxima and minima).

questions.prompt: State how the resultant displacement at a point is found from the displacement–distance graphs of two superposed waves.
questions.answer: Add the displacements of the two waves at that point, taking account of their directions.

title: Young's double slit and diffraction gratings

questions.prompt: State the equation relating wavelength, fringe spacing, slit separation and slit-to-screen distance for Young's double-slit experiment.
questions.answer: λ = ax/D (equivalently x = λD/a), where x is the fringe spacing, a is the slit separation and D is the slit-to-screen distance.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the fringe spacing.
questions.answer: The distance between the centres of adjacent bright fringes (maxima) on the screen.

questions.prompt: State the effect of increasing the slit separation on the fringe spacing, with all other quantities unchanged.
questions.answer: The fringe spacing decreases.

questions.prompt: State the effect of moving the screen further from the slits on the fringe spacing.
questions.answer: The fringe spacing increases.

questions.prompt: State the condition under which x = λD/a applies.
questions.answer: The slit separation must be much smaller than the slit-to-screen distance (a ≪ D).

questions.prompt: State the equation for the maxima produced by a diffraction grating.
questions.answer: d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing, θ is the angle to the normal and n is the order of the maximum.

questions.prompt: State one difference between the interference pattern from a double slit and that from a diffraction grating.
questions.answer: A grating produces much sharper (narrower) bright maxima at well-defined angles; a double slit produces broad fringes.

questions.prompt: State what Young's double-slit experiment demonstrated about light.
questions.answer: That light behaves as a wave (it produces an interference pattern).

questions.prompt: Define a stationary (standing) wave.
questions.answer: A wave formed by the superposition of two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Define a node and an antinode.
questions.answer: A node is a point of zero displacement (zero amplitude); an antinode is a point of maximum displacement (maximum amplitude).

questions.prompt: State the separation between adjacent nodes in terms of the wavelength.
State one difference between a stationary wave and a progressive wave.
questions.answer: A stationary wave does not transfer energy along its length, whereas a progressive wave does transfer energy.

questions.prompt: State one similarity between a stationary wave and a progressive wave.
questions.answer: They have the same frequency and wavelength (the stationary wave is formed from progressive waves of that frequency and wavelength).

questions.prompt: State the wavelength of the fundamental mode (first harmonic) on a string of length L fixed at both ends.
questions.answer: λ = 2L.

questions.prompt: State the wavelength of the first harmonic in a pipe of length L closed at one end and open at the other.
questions.answer: λ = 4L.

questions.prompt: State the wavelength of the first harmonic in a pipe of length L open at both ends.
questions.answer: λ = 2L.

questions.prompt: State how the speed of sound in air can be determined using a resonance tube and a tuning fork.
questions.answer: Find two successive resonance lengths; their separation is λ/2, giving λ, then use v = fλ with the tuning-fork frequency.

questions.prompt: Describe the displacement–distance graph of a stationary wave.
questions.answer: A sine curve whose amplitude is zero at each node and maximum at each antinode.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a photon.
questions.answer: A quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the energy of a photon in terms of its frequency.
questions.answer: E = hf.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the energy of a photon in terms of its wavelength.
questions.answer: E = hc/λ.

questions.prompt: State the value of the Planck constant.
Define the electronvolt.
questions.answer: The energy gained (or lost) by an electron when it moves through a potential difference of 1 V.

questions.prompt: State the value of one electronvolt in joules.
State the equation relating the threshold potential difference of an LED to the wavelength of the light it emits.
questions.answer: eV = hc/λ (so h = eVλ/c).

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the threshold voltage of an LED.
questions.answer: The minimum potential difference across the LED at which it just begins to emit light.

questions.prompt: State how the Planck constant can be determined from measurements of threshold voltage and wavelength for several LEDs.
questions.answer: Plot eV against 1/λ; the gradient is hc, so h = gradient ÷ c.

questions.prompt: Define the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of a frequency above the threshold frequency is incident on it.

questions.prompt: Define the work function of a metal.
questions.answer: The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of the metal.

questions.prompt: Define the threshold frequency.
questions.answer: The minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that can cause photoelectric emission from a metal surface.

questions.prompt: State Einstein's photoelectric equation.
questions.answer: hf = φ + KEmax (photon energy = work function + maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron).

questions.prompt: State the nature of the interaction between a photon and a surface electron in the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: A one-to-one interaction: one photon is absorbed by one electron.

questions.prompt: State how the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons depends on the intensity of the incident radiation above the threshold frequency.
questions.answer: It is independent of the intensity.

questions.prompt: State how the rate of emission of photoelectrons depends on the intensity of the incident radiation above the threshold frequency.
questions.answer: It is directly proportional to the intensity.

questions.prompt: Explain why the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by the wave model of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: A wave would transfer energy gradually, so emission would occur after a time delay and at any frequency once enough energy had built up; in practice emission is instantaneous and only occurs above a threshold frequency.

questions.prompt: State what is observed when ultraviolet light shines on a negatively charged zinc plate.
questions.answer: The plate loses its negative charge, because electrons are emitted from its surface.

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing the frequency of the incident radiation increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.
questions.answer: Each photon has more energy (E = hf), so after overcoming the same work function the electron has more kinetic energy left.

questions.prompt: State the de Broglie equation.
questions.answer: λ = h/p, where p is the momentum of the particle.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by wave–particle duality.
questions.answer: The idea that electromagnetic radiation and particles can both show wave-like and particle-like behaviour, depending on the experiment.

questions.prompt: State the experimental evidence that electrons can behave as waves.
questions.answer: Electrons passing through a thin slice of polycrystalline graphite produce a diffraction pattern of concentric rings.

questions.prompt: Explain why the diffraction pattern produced by electrons passing through graphite shows that electrons behave as waves.
questions.answer: Diffraction is a wave property; the rings arise from constructive and destructive interference of electron waves scattered by the regularly spaced atoms in the graphite.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the de Broglie wavelength of an electron when its momentum increases.
questions.answer: It decreases (λ ∝ 1/p).

questions.prompt: State why electrons with energies of the order of 100 eV are suitable for investigating atomic spacing.
questions.answer: Their de Broglie wavelength is of the same order as atomic spacing (about 10⁻¹⁰ m), so significant diffraction occurs.
